title: The Woodpile and the Last: from Hadjin in the Taurus to an orthopedic bench in Buenos Aires
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Hadjin, the Town in the Taurus

stops.name: Hadjin, birth in the mountain town
stops.date_confidence: Year attested in the AGBU interview, spoken by Shorjian at 102. No month or day is recorded anywhere; the date defaults to 1 January. No birth register survives.
stops.campa: High in the Taurus of Cilicia stands Hadjin, some thirty thousand Armenians, six churches, a dialect of its own, settled in part by people who came up here after the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia fell in 1375. Arshag Shorjian is born in it in 1898. The Ottoman administration files the place as a kaza of the sanjak of Kozan in the vilayet of Adana. The people who live in it know it as high ground in a country that has already ended once. His birth year reaches the world by one route only: his own mouth, a hundred and two years later, in Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: Virtual Genocide Memorial, entry for Kaza Hacin, sanjak of Kozan, vilayet of Adana
sources: David Zenian, 'The Armenians of Argentina,' AGBU Magazine, November 2000

stops.name: Hadjin, the house that is not named
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The source names the town and nothing smaller; the year here marks the middle of his time in it, not an event.
stops.campa: The town is named in the record; the street is not, and the house is not. Shorjian passes five years somewhere inside Hadjin's stacked stone quarters, in the Armenian of the mountains, thirty thousand people and six churches in a town he will never see again after the age of five. Of this household nothing whatever survives: not the father's trade, not the mother's name, not whether there were brothers, not even the street the house stood on. The first five years of the life are a town and a year and no more.
suggested_refs: The Armenian quarters of Hadjin before 1909, unmapped in any reachable source
sources: saint_blaise.journey.json, stop 'Sebastea, birth in Lesser Armenia'

stops.name: Hadjin, the family goes down from the mountain
stops.date_confidence: Year attested in the AGBU interview; no month given, defaulted to 1 January. No reason for the move is recorded.
stops.campa: In 1903 the Shorjians leave the mountain for the provincial capital on the plain. The boy is about five. No reason is given for the move in the only source that mentions it, and none is invented here. What can be said is what the map says: they come down out of a defensible Armenian town that outsiders reach with difficulty, and settle in a mixed commercial city on open ground, six years before the open ground matters. Hadjin will stand another seventeen years. He will never see it again.
suggested_refs: The Hadjin to Adana road through the Kozan defiles

stops.name: Adana, arrival in the provincial capital
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month unrecorded and set here only to order the stop after the departure from Hadjin.
stops.campa: Adana is the capital of the vilayet, a cotton and commerce city on the Seyhan, with a large Armenian population working in trade, weaving, and the crafts. The family arrives in 1903 and takes its place in the Armenian quarter. The AGBU interview establishes the move and stops there; it names no address, no occupation, no parish. What the city offers a boy of five is schooling, a language spoken in shops as well as at home, and six years in which nothing recorded happens to him at all.
suggested_refs: The Armenian commercial quarter of Adana before 1909

stops.name: Adana, the churches of the quarter
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Sourp Boghos Bedros is documented as an Adana Armenian church of the period; no source connects the Shorjian family to it or to any named parish.
stops.campa: Sourp Boghos Bedros, Saints Peter and Paul, stands among the principal Armenian churches of Adana in these years. Its exact address in the old quarter is not fixed in any reachable source, and no source says the Shorjians worshipped there or anywhere. The church is set down here as what it is: a building of the sort the family lived among, at the only distance the record allows. In three years the quarter around it will burn, and the buildings will be better documented in their destruction than they ever were standing.
suggested_refs: Sourp Boghos Bedros Armenian church, Adana, location unfixed in reachable sources
sources: General Adana massacre historiography; no direct link to Shorjian confirmed

stops.name: Adana vilayet, the massacres of April 1909
stops.date_confidence: Attested as regional history. Not a claim about Shorjian personally.
stops.campa: In April 1909 the killing runs across the whole vilayet. The estimates that survive give twenty to thirty thousand Armenians dead and about thirteen hundred Assyrians. In Hadjin, the town the family left six years earlier, the monastery is destroyed and will later be rebuilt as a school. This is the arithmetic of a province, not of a household. The household appears in the record only because one member of it was eleven years old, survived, lived to a hundred and two, and was asked a question in Buenos Aires ninety-one years later.
stops.quote_source: David Zenian, 'The Armenians of Argentina,' AGBU Magazine, November 2000, quoted phrase in the journalist's narration
suggested_refs: Armenian Genocide Museum-Institute materials on the Adana massacres of April 1909
sources: Virtual Genocide Memorial, entry for Kaza Hacin

stops.name: Adana, the pile of firewood
stops.date_confidence: Month attested as April 1909 in the AGBU interview; the day is not recorded and is set here only to place the stop within the massacre days.
stops.campa: Armed men come into the house. They kill Shorjian's grandfather and his uncle. The boy is small enough to get under a pile of firewood, and stays there, and is not found. He is about eleven. The grandfather and the uncle are the only two members of his family the record ever names, and it names them as the dead. Everything else known about this man begins on the other side of that woodpile: the port, the boat, the orphanage, the trade, the seventy years of bench work in a city he had never heard of.
stops.quote: I was a little boy then, but I can never forget that day. They came into our house and killed my grandfather and uncle. I was very small and was able to hide under a pile of firewood.
stops.quote_source: Arshag Shorjian to David Zenian, AGBU Magazine, November 2000, interviewed at the Armenian home for the elderly, Buenos Aires
suggested_refs: The unlocated Shorjian house in Adana, April 1909

stops.name: Adana, the neighbours who kept them
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Shorjian's own words as the aftermath of April 1909; no month is given and June is set only to follow the massacre.
stops.campa: The few who came through are protected by Turkish neighbours. Shorjian says this himself, without qualification, in an interview given at a hundred and two in a city whose Armenian community was assembled out of this event. He says it in the same breath as the killing of his grandfather and his uncle, and the article softens neither half. In the sentence that follows he dates the next thing that happens to him to 1914, where the histories put 1915. His own year stands here, and the gap between the two is marked rather than corrected.
stops.quote: The few of us who survived were protected by some of our Turkish neighbors but the situation deteriorated again with the start of the second wave of massacres in 1914.
stops.quote_source: Arshag Shorjian to David Zenian, AGBU Magazine, November 2000
suggested_refs: The 1909 to 1914 interval in Adana, undocumented for the Shorjian family

stops.name: Adana, the five years nobody wrote down
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The interval 1909 to 1914 is empty in every reachable source; the date marks its midpoint only.
stops.campa: Between the woodpile and the deportation lie five years about which no source says anything at all. Presumably the family stays in Adana, because the deportation narrative starts from Adana; presumably the boy goes on being a boy there. Neither presumption is attested. He is eleven at one end of the silence and sixteen at the other. His schooling in that time is unrecorded. So is the question of how a household that had lost two men fed itself, and so is anything he may have understood then about what had happened in the house.
suggested_refs: Gap: no source covers the Shorjian family between April 1909 and 1914
sources: Gap; no source found for this interval

stops.name: Adana, the road out
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the departure point: AGBU names only the destination, Mersin. Adana is inferred because the family was living there. Year attested as 1914 by AGBU and by Shorjian himself; the standard chronology of the Cilician deportations gives 1915, and the conflict is flagged, not resolved.
stops.campa: He is put on the road with the others, no family named as walking beside him. The source names the destination and not the origin, so Adana is inference: the family was living there, and no other starting point is named. He is sixteen. The year he gives is 1914; the histories of the Cilician deportations say 1915. Both dates stand here, uncorrected against each other, because the only witness to this particular march is the man who walked it and he said 1914.
stops.quote_source: David Zenian, 'The Armenians of Argentina,' AGBU Magazine, November 2000, quoted phrase in the journalist's narration
suggested_refs: The Adana to Mersin road, route of the 1914 deportation as Shorjian dates it

stops.name: Tarsus, the waypoint on the road
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Tarsus lies directly on the Adana to Mersin road and is the likeliest waypoint, but no source names it for Shorjian; the date is placed only to order the stop.
stops.campa: Between Adana and the sea lies Tarsus, and anyone marched from one to the other passes through it. No source puts Shorjian there by name. This stop is a reconstruction, because a march is a line and not two dots: the road is an old one, already a fixed route between the two cities for centuries before him. It is about forty kilometres from here to the water, a day or two on foot. That much is known about the geometry, and nothing at all about the man inside the column.
suggested_refs: The Roman road from Adana through Tarsus to Mersin
sources: Geographic reconstruction; no source names this waypoint for Shorjian

stops.name: Mersin, the end of the march
stops.date_confidence: Destination attested by AGBU; year 1914 as the source states, with the 1915 conventional chronology flagged. Month unrecorded.
stops.campa: The march ends at Mersin, the Mediterranean port that serves the province of Adana. The AGBU sentence is short and carries the whole of it: the long march to the Turkish port of Mersin and the journey on a French boat to Beirut. No family member is mentioned as being with him at any point after the killings of 1909, and what waits for him in Lebanon is an orphanage, which argues against there being anyone. He arrives at the water alone, so far as the record permits anyone to say.
suggested_refs: The port of Mersin, terminus of the Adana deportation route

stops.name: Mersin harbour, the French boat
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he sailed from Mersin to Beirut on a French vessel; no ship name, no sailing date, no manifest located. Day set only to order the stop.
stops.campa: A French boat takes him off. That is the whole of what is known: the nationality of the flag and the two ends of the passage. No ship name, no sailing date, no manifest, no passenger list, nothing that any archive has been found to hold. In 1914 the French merchant lines still work the Levant coast out of Mersin as they have for decades, and one of their hulls carries a sixteen-year-old shoemaker who is not yet a shoemaker down the coast to Beirut.
suggested_refs: Gap: no ship name or manifest located for the Mersin to Beirut passage

stops.name: Beirut, the harbour under the Ottoman flag
stops.date_confidence: Arrival attested by AGBU; no date given, month set only to follow the sailing.
stops.campa: Beirut in 1914 is still Ottoman, capital of the vilayet of Beirut, and it is also the place the relief operations work out of: consulates, missions, orphanages, the whole apparatus that assembles around displaced people faster than any government does. Shorjian comes ashore into it. He has crossed from one province of the same empire to another, and the crossing has changed everything, because in the second province there are institutions willing to feed him.
suggested_refs: The port of Beirut, vilayet of Beirut, point of arrival for displaced Armenians in 1914

stops.name: Jounieh, the orphanage
stops.date_confidence: Five years in an orphanage at Jounieh is attested; AGBU gives no years at all. The start is reconstructed from the 1914 arrival. The orphanage is not named or attributed to any organization in the article.
stops.campa: North of Beirut on the coast sits Jounieh, and in Jounieh an orphanage takes him in. The article says that much and no more: it does not name the institution, and it does not say who ran it. The research pool that fed this journey attached the Near East Relief system to it; the attachment is not in the source and is removed here. What is in the source is the duration, five years, and the two things he takes out of them, which are a language and a trade.
suggested_refs: Gap: the Jounieh orphanage is unnamed and unattributed in the only source

stops.name: Jounieh, learning Arabic
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he learned Arabic at the orphanage; no year is given, and this one marks the middle of the five years only.
stops.campa: He learns Arabic here. It is the language of the country that took him in, and he keeps it as long as he has any use for it: nothing in the record says he spoke a word of it after 1926, when he sailed for a city that worked in Spanish. The article does not say who taught him, or whether the teaching was formal, or what else was taught alongside it. What it does say is that he named the language himself, at a hundred and two, as one of the two things Jounieh gave him. The other was the trade.
suggested_refs: Armenian orphan schooling in Lebanon during the First World War

stops.name: Jounieh, the shoemaker's bench
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he learned shoemaking at the orphanage; no year given, set at the middle of the five years.
stops.campa: The other thing Jounieh gives him is a last, a knife, an awl, and the method. Orphanages of the period teach trades, on the reasoning that a boy with a trade stops needing an orphanage. He takes shoemaking. Later, in Argentina, he will narrow it to orthopedic work, shoes built for feet that do not match the standard forms, and he will still be doing it at a hundred. He is about seventeen when this is settled, and the institution that settles it has never been named in any source reached.
suggested_refs: Trade instruction in Armenian orphanages of the Lebanese coast

stops.name: Aintab, the orphanage that will not fit the date
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction pin. Near East Relief secondary sources date the founding of the orphanage network at Aintab to after the armistice and its relocation to Jounieh to 1920; AGBU has Shorjian in a Jounieh orphanage from 1914. Not resolved.
stops.campa: A pin set for a problem rather than an event. Secondary accounts of the Near East Relief network put its orphanage at Aintab after the armistice, moving to Jounieh only in 1920 for safety. AGBU has Shorjian inside a Jounieh orphanage six years before that. Either the interview's chronology is compressed by nine decades of distance, or his orphanage was some other institution entirely, and no reachable source decides it. Both timelines stand here, and neither is adjudicated.
suggested_refs: Near East Relief records of the Aintab to Jounieh orphanage relocation, 1920
sources: Secondary web sources on Near East Relief orphanages in Lebanon, contrasted with AGBU Magazine, November 2000

stops.name: Jounieh, the five years end
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction by arithmetic only: 1914 plus the attested five years. No source states this year. One lens of the research gave c. 1915 to 1920 for the same span; that conflict is recorded and not resolved.
stops.campa: 1914 plus five is 1919, and that is the entire basis for this date. No source gives it. He walks out of the institution at about twenty-one with Arabic, a trade, and no recorded family anywhere on earth. Behind him the war has ended and Cilicia is briefly French. Ahead of him lie seven years the record does not touch. The exit is marked here because a journey needs one, and marked as arithmetic because that is what it is. One lens of the research gave the same span as 1915 to 1920 instead; neither version is sourced, and the disagreement is left standing on the page.
suggested_refs: Gap: no source states when Shorjian left the Jounieh orphanage
sources: Reconstructed from AGBU Magazine, November 2000, which states five years and gives no exit date

stops.name: Hadjin, the town taken down
stops.date_confidence: Attested: about 8,000 survivors returned in 1919, Kemalist troops besieged the town from March 1920, and it fell that October. Whether Shorjian learned of it is not recorded.
stops.campa: About eight thousand survivors go back up to Hadjin in 1919. France then cedes Cilicia, and from March 1920 Kemalist troops sit around the town; it falls in October and only a few hundred get out. The place Shorjian was born in stops existing as an Armenian town in the same year he is somewhere in Lebanon with no address the record can find. Nothing says he heard. The site is renamed Saimbeyli, and the name Hadjin survives in compatriotic unions kept up by people who were carried out of it as children.
suggested_refs: Virtual Genocide Memorial, Kaza Hacin: the 1919 return and the siege of March to October 1920

segments.name: The Undocumented Years and the Crossing

stops.name: Lebanon, the seven years no source covers
stops.date_confidence: Gap. Nothing is known of 1919 to 1926; the date marks the midpoint of the emptiness only.
stops.campa: Between the orphanage gate and the Argentine coast lie about seven years in which no source says where he lived, whether he cut shoes in Lebanon, how he paid for a ticket, or when the uncle in Buenos Aires had gone out. He is twenty-one at one end of this and twenty-eight at the other. The gap is stated as a gap here, and nothing is put in it. A life this thinly recorded is mostly gap; what makes this one worth marking is that it is the stretch in which he must have decided to cross an ocean.
suggested_refs: Gap: no source covers Shorjian between c. 1919 and 1926
sources: Gap; no source found covering this period

stops.name: Beirut, the presumed embarkation
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. AGBU names no port of departure and no shipping record has been located; Beirut is inferred from his residence in Lebanon.
stops.campa: If he sailed for the Americas from anywhere, he sailed from Beirut, which is the port his country of residence has and the one the emigration used. The source does not say so. No shipping record has been found. The pin is a reconstruction and is labelled one. He goes down the same quays he came up twelve years earlier off a French boat. Nothing before this in the record is his own doing: the woodpile, the march, the boat and the orphanage were all done to him or arranged for him. Leaving is the first move the record lets him make.
suggested_refs: Gap: no manifest or embarkation record located for the 1926 crossing

stops.name: Marseille, the presumed transit
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction based on the standard emigrant routing of the 1920s; not attested for Shorjian in any source.
stops.campa: Levantine emigrants bound for South America in the 1920s go through Marseille, transferring there from the Mediterranean lines to the transatlantic ones. It is the ordinary shape of the route and nothing more; no source puts Shorjian in France. The pin stands as the probable middle of a crossing whose two ends are known and whose middle is not. Marseille in these years is thick with Armenians who have made the same passage and stopped there instead of going on.
suggested_refs: Marseille as transshipment port for Levantine emigration to South America, 1920s
sources: Reconstruction based on typical emigrant routing of the 1920s; not directly attested for Shorjian

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, landfall
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by AGBU; no month, day, ship, or manifest is recorded and none has been located.
stops.campa: He comes ashore at Buenos Aires in 1926, twenty-eight years old, to join an uncle already settled here. The article gives the year and the uncle and nothing else: not the ship, not the month, not the uncle's name or trade or address. He is one of an estimated ten thousand Armenian refugees who reach Argentina between 1909 and 1938, which is to say he arrives inside a movement large enough to be counted and small enough that the counting is done in round numbers.
suggested_refs: Gap: no Argentine immigration file or passenger record located for Arshag Shorjian

stops.name: Puerto Madero, the docks of the Ottoman emigration
stops.date_confidence: Canonical atlas pin inherited from emin_arslan.journey.json. The 1910 event is attested for Arslan; Shorjian's own use of these docks in 1926 is inference from the port's function.
stops.campa: Sixteen years before, at these docks, a crowd of four thousand met the steamer Chili to receive Emin Arslan, Druze emir and consul general of the Ottoman Empire, mobilized in part by the Sociedad Joven Otomana. The Ottoman subjects of Buenos Aires were already organized enough in 1910 to fill a quay. Shorjian lands into that arrangement in 1926: Syrian, Lebanese, and Armenian emigres from a single empire, disembarking at a single port, sorted afterward by which massacre they left.
suggested_refs: The Chili docks at Puerto Madero, 29 October 1910
sources: emin_arslan.journey.json, stop 'Puerto Madero, the Chili docks to a crowd of four thousand'

stops.name: Hotel de Inmigrantes, the receiving house
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The building opened in 1911 and processed arrivals in this period; AGBU says only that Shorjian came to join his uncle and does not mention it.
stops.campa: New arrivals to Buenos Aires in these years pass through the Hotel de Inmigrantes on Avenida Antartida Argentina, a state receiving house opened in 1911 with dormitories, a dining hall, and an employment office. Whether Shorjian went through it is not confirmed anywhere; a man met at the quay by an uncle may not have needed it. The pin is reconstruction. The building still stands and is now the Museo de la Inmigracion, which is more than can be said for anything else on this journey east of Marseille.
suggested_refs: Hotel de Inmigrantes, Av. Antartida Argentina 1335, now the Museo de la Inmigracion
sources: Reconstruction based on standard Argentine immigration processing of the period; not directly attested for Shorjian

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the uncle's house
stops.date_confidence: The uncle is attested by AGBU; his name, address, trade, and date of emigration are all unrecorded. The month is set to follow the landing.
stops.campa: There is an uncle. He is in Argentina before Shorjian and he is the reason Shorjian is in Argentina, and that is the entire content of the record concerning him: no name, no street, no trade, no date of his own crossing. The research pool offered a claim that early Armenian arrivals lived in conventillos around San Juan and Jujuy, sourced to AGBU; the article contains no such passage, and the claim is dropped here rather than carried. An uncle, then, and a door that opened.
suggested_refs: Gap: the uncle in Argentina is unnamed and unlocated in every source

stops.name: Armenia Street, the lot bought in 1922
stops.date_confidence: The purchase of the Acevedo Street lot in 1922 and the later renaming of the street to Armenia are attested by AGBU. Shorjian's own presence there is not recorded.
stops.campa: Four years before he lands, the community buys a lot on Acevedo Street. The church and the institutions go up on it, and in time the city renames the street Armenia. This is the one settlement locus the AGBU article actually names, and it is where a man arriving in 1926 with no family but an uncle would go to find people from Hadjin. Nothing records that Shorjian went. The address is set down because a colectividad is a place before it is a statistic, and this was the place.
suggested_refs: The Acevedo Street lot bought in 1922, later Armenia Street, Palermo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the news had come eleven years early
stops.date_confidence: The La Nota reporting of August 1915 is attested in emin_arslan.journey.json. The date here marks an anniversary of that reporting within Shorjian's first year in the city, not an event in his life.
stops.campa: In August 1915, a week after founding his weekly La Nota, Emin Arslan printed in Buenos Aires the first general word of the deportations and killings then running against the Ottoman Empire's Armenian subjects. He had been the Sultan's consul general in this city from 1910 to 1914. Alberto Gerchunoff wrote for the same paper. Shorjian arrives in 1926 into a city where what was done to him had already been set in type by an Ottoman ex-consul, in Spanish, for readers who had never seen Cilicia.
suggested_refs: La Nota, Buenos Aires, number of 21 August 1915
sources: emin_arslan.journey.json, stop 'Buenos Aires, La Nota carries the first word of the Armenian extermination'
alberto_gerchunoff.journey.json, stop 'Buenos Aires, La Nación at San Martin 350'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the general who died too soon to be met
stops.date_confidence: Czetz's Armenian descent is attested by a Hungarian National Library source and by the Armenian Embassy in Argentina, which gives his Armenian name as Hovhannes Tzetzian. He died in Buenos Aires in 1904. No connection to Shorjian exists or is claimed.
stops.campa: He arrives into a community still building itself. The lot on Acevedo Street was bought four years before he lands, and the church on it will not be consecrated for another twelve; in between, the ten thousand keep arriving, family by family, the same way he came, off a boat with an address and nothing else. No membership roll survives that names him, no minutes of a meeting, no subscription list. What can be said is only what is true of thousands of the others: a man walks into a half-built neighbourhood carrying a trade and a language nobody here yet speaks, and the neighbourhood absorbs him the way it absorbed the rest.
suggested_refs: Queue entry for janos_czetz; Armenian Embassy in Argentina on Hovhannes Tzetzian

stops.name: Once, where the colectividades overlap
stops.date_confidence: Canonical atlas pin inherited from alberto_gerchunoff.journey.json, whose 1933 stop is attested for Gerchunoff. Shorjian's presence in Once is not recorded and is not claimed.
stops.campa: Once is where Alberto Gerchunoff's file puts the Jewish civic and antifascist press of the 1930s, and it is also, in the same decades, a concentration point for the city's Middle Eastern and Armenian trade. Two diasporas of the same century, both arriving out of empires that had decided against them, working the same twelve blocks. Nothing places Shorjian here. Gerchunoff's file dates its Once stop to 1933, and this pin borrows that year. It marks an overlap on the map and not a meeting between men.
suggested_refs: Once, Buenos Aires, in the 1930s
sources: alberto_gerchunoff.journey.json, stop 'Buenos Aires, Once, the end of assimilation'

stops.name: Palermo, the cathedral consecrated
stops.date_confidence: The consecration of the Cathedral of San Gregorio el Iluminador in 1938 and its architect Israel Arslan are attested in general sources. Shorjian's attendance is not documented anywhere.
stops.campa: On Armenia 1353, the Cathedral of San Gregorio el Iluminador is consecrated in 1938, designed by Israel Arslan: the community's first permanent church, sixteen years after the lot was bought. By this year the migration that carried Shorjian is finished, the ten thousand are in, and the buildings begin. He is forty and has been cutting shoes here for twelve years. Whether he stood in the crowd at the consecration nobody wrote down, and this account does not put him there either.
suggested_refs: Cathedral of San Gregorio el Iluminador, Armenia 1353, Palermo, consecrated 1938
sources: General history of the Cathedral San Gregorio el Iluminador; Shorjian's personal connection not attested

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the workshop
stops.date_confidence: The trade and the city are attested; no workshop address survives in any source, and the year marks the establishment of the working life rather than a documented opening.
stops.campa: He works as a shoemaker and narrows to orthopedic work: shoes built to a foot that no factory form fits, made one at a time for people who cannot buy them off a shelf. No address for the workshop survives. The trade is the through-line of the whole life, learned in an orphanage in Lebanon at seventeen because the institution taught trades, practised in Argentina for seventy-two years because it turned out to be worth practising. It is the only thing he ever says he was good at.
suggested_refs: Gap: no workshop address for Shorjian survives in any source

stops.name: Buenos Aires, no wife and no children
stops.date_confidence: Attested by AGBU that he never married; the source gives no elaboration and no date attaches to a negative. The year marks the middle of the working life only.
stops.campa: He never marries. The article states it flat and adds nothing, and nothing is added here. He was eleven when his grandfather and his uncle were killed in the house, sixteen when he was marched to the sea, and an institution raised him after that. Then he lived seventy-four years in a city across the Atlantic and founded no household in it. No reason is recorded anywhere. The only man who could have given one sat for an interview at a hundred and two and did not give it.
suggested_refs: Gap: no source elaborates on Shorjian's unmarried life

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the hundredth birthday
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the municipal social security department gave him a reception for his hundredth birthday; the venue is not specified and the city centre stands here as an approximate civic reference point. The year derives from his stated 1898 birth.
stops.campa: At a hundred the city holds a reception for him. The municipal social security department does it. The venue is not recorded, so the pin sits on the civic centre as an approximation and says so. He is still working, and has been for seventy-two years. The town he was born in stopped carrying its own name in 1920. No text or programme from the reception survives, so what was said about him there is unknown. Two years later he tells a journalist what he remembers of the day: that he had never had a birthday like it, and that the pay was not good.
stops.quote: I had never had a birthday like that. I would have continued working but the pay was not good.
stops.quote_source: Arshag Shorjian to David Zenian, AGBU Magazine, November 2000, on the reception given by the Buenos Aires municipal social security department
suggested_refs: Records of the Buenos Aires municipal social security department reception, c. 1998

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the last pair
stops.date_confidence: Derived from the attested statement that he worked until the age of 100, taken with his stated 1898 birth year. No source records a date of retirement.
stops.campa: He stops at a hundred, and by his own account he stops because the pay is not good, not because the hands go. Seventy-two years at the bench in one city, ending in a year he does not mark and nobody records. There is no last customer named, no shop closed on a date, no notice anywhere. The work simply ends and two years later a journalist finds him in a home for the elderly, walking briskly, not wearing glasses, willing to come back for the right wage.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Armenian home for the elderly
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested by AGBU; the home's name and address are not given in the article and no other source names them.
stops.campa: In July 2000 he moves into the Armenian home for the elderly in Buenos Aires. The institution is not named and its address is not given, so the pin sits on the city. He is a hundred and two. Eighty-six years after an orphanage on the Lebanese coast took in a boy off a French boat, an Armenian institution in another hemisphere takes in the same man, and the community that received the ten thousand between 1909 and 1938 is still standing and still has a bed.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, David Zenian asks
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the interview appears in the November 2000 issue of AGBU Magazine. The exact day of the interview is not given.
stops.campa: David Zenian comes to the home for AGBU Magazine's Ola Buenos Aires feature and finds a man of a hundred and two in reasonable health, walking briskly, not needing glasses. Over the course of it Shorjian gives the Adana killings, the march, the French boat, the orphanage, and the seventy-two years of shoes. This afternoon is the entire documentary basis of his existence. Everything known about him is known because one journalist walked into one building in one month and asked.
stops.quote: I might get back to work if I find a well-paying job. I made orthopedic shoes all my life, and I'm still very good at my profession.
stops.quote_source: Arshag Shorjian to David Zenian, AGBU Magazine, November 2000, spoken at 102
suggested_refs: David Zenian, 'The Armenians of Argentina,' AGBU Magazine, November 2000

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the line at the door
stops.date_confidence: Attested as the closing line of the interview, introduced by Zenian as what Shorjian told him as he left. The day is set only to place it after the interview stop.
stops.campa: Zenian records it as the thing said to him on the way out. It is the last sentence of Arshag Shorjian that any source preserves, and it is not about himself: it is about the people who came out of the same years and built the community that is now feeding him. A man who lost a grandfather and an uncle in one room, a town, a country, and a family he never names, closing an interview by putting the price in the plural. He is a hundred and two, he has been in Argentina for seventy-four years, and the word he uses for the people around him is us.
stops.quote: The Armenians of this country are the product of a generation which paid a high price to keep its identity and that in itself has kept us unique. Our collective memory has not faded.
stops.quote_source: Arshag Shorjian to David Zenian, AGBU Magazine, November 2000, closing line of the interview

stops.name: Buenos Aires, no death date
stops.date_confidence: Gap. No death date, place, or circumstance has been located; the date here is a placeholder immediately after the last attested trace and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: Nothing after November 2000. No obituary, no death notice, no cemetery record, no follow-up article, nothing. He was a hundred and two when Zenian left him, so death presumably came within a few years, and presumably is not a fact. Whether he lies in the Armenian section of a Buenos Aires cemetery, as the community's custom would have it, is unattested. The journey ends by running out of sources rather than by reaching a grave, and that is stated here instead of estimating one.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, no plaque and no street
stops.date_confidence: Gap. No monument, plaque, street name, or memorial naming him has been found; the date is a placeholder and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: No monument carries his name, no plaque, no street. He wrote no book; no memoir, article, or recording by him has been found in any search, so there is nothing to edit and nothing to translate. He is commemorated only in the aggregate, as one of the interviewees standing in for a generation of Adana survivors who built a community in another hemisphere. The record of his existence is one magazine article and five sentences he spoke inside it. A Facebook post naming another Shorjian out of Hadjin was tested and set aside: same rare surname, same town, no documented link, and a group post is below the floor this record works to.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the trace that stayed online
stops.date_confidence: The profile's presence in AGBU's online archive is attested by the archive itself. The date marks persistence rather than an event. A research-pool claim that scholars cite the piece was tested and no citation was found; it is not asserted here.
stops.campa: The one surviving afterlife is digital. The November 2000 profile stays up in AGBU's online archive, where it can still be read: a primary oral testimony taken while the witnesses to 1909 were alive to give one, which by 2000 meant a very short list of people. The research behind this journey looked for scholarly citation of the piece and found none, so none is claimed. It sits there, unfootnoted, holding the only account of a life that ran from the Taurus to the Rio de la Plata.

stops.name: Saimbeyli, the town under the other name
stops.date_confidence: Present-day identification attested: Hadjin is the modern Saimbeyli, Adana Province, Turkey, at 37.9846 north, 36.0888 east. The date marks the present, not an event.
stops.campa: The town is called Saimbeyli now, in the province of Adana, and it holds a few thousand people. The monastery destroyed in 1909 was rebuilt as a school. Of the thirty thousand Armenians and six churches, the record keeps the numbers and the site keeps neither. The compatriotic unions of Hadjin still meet, in Lebanon and elsewhere, kept up by the descendants of people carried out. Arshag Shorjian was born here in 1898 and left at five, and the only thing he is known to have said about it is where it was.
